title: THE RELATION OF STRENGTH OF STIMULUS TO RAPIDITY OF HABIT-FORMATION
authors: Robert M. Yerkes and John D. Dodson, 1908
research_question: 1. Does the strength of an electric stimulus influence the rapidity with which dancing mice acquire a white-black visual discrimination habit? 2. If so, what particular strength of stimulus is most favorable to the acquisition of this habit?

participants.description: Dancing mice, 6-8 weeks old at the beginning of training. Comprised of males and females.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A wooden discrimination box (94 cm long, 30 cm wide, 11.5 cm deep) divided into a nest-box, an entrance chamber, and two electric boxes (one white, one black). The white and black cards were interchangeable. Electric shock was delivered via wires on the floor of the electric boxes.

Electric shock stimulus of varying strengths, generated by a Porter inductorium. Calibrated in 'units of stimulation' (Martin's unit). Strengths used: 125±10, 300±25, 500±50, 135, 195, 255, 375, 420 units.

Visual discrimination conditions (white vs. black electric boxes) varied in difficulty by altering brightness difference: Set I (medium difficulty), Set II (easy/great difference), Set III (difficult/slight difference). This was achieved by modifying internal cardboard configurations and open space for light entry.

measures.instrument: Number of tests required to achieve a 'perfect habit' (choosing correctly in every test on three consecutive days).
Number of errors made in each series of ten tests.

findings.mechanism: An intermediate strength of electrical stimulus (300 units) is most favorable for habit acquisition under medium discrimination difficulty, demonstrating the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: neither a weak nor a strong electrical stimulus is as favorable to the acquisition of the white-black habit as is a medium stimulus.

findings.antecedent: Electric stimulus strength (125 units, Set I, medium discrimination)
findings.mechanism: Weak stimulus provides inadequate motivation for avoidance.
findings.quote: the stimulus was too weak to furnish an adequate motive for the avoidance of the black box

findings.antecedent: Electric stimulus strength (300 units, Set I, medium discrimination)
findings.mechanism: Medium stimulus provides optimal motivation for avoidance.
findings.quote: the medium stimulus was much more favorable to the acquirement of the white-black visual discrimination habit.

findings.antecedent: Electric stimulus strength (500 units, Set I, medium discrimination)
findings.mechanism: Strong stimulus leads to slower learning, possibly due to excessive arousal or distress.
findings.quote: All of the mice in this case learned more slowly than did those which were trained with the medium strength of stimulus.

findings.mechanism: When discrimination is easy, learning rapidity increases with stimulus strength up to the highest tested (420 units).
findings.quote: the rapidity of learning in this set of experiments increased as the strength of the stimulus increased.

findings.antecedent: Electric stimulus strength (135 units, Set II, easy discrimination)
findings.mechanism: Weakest stimulus leads to slower learning even with easy discrimination.
findings.quote: The weakest stimulus (135 units) gave the slowest rate of learning

findings.antecedent: Electric stimulus strength (420 units, Set II, easy discrimination)
findings.mechanism: Strongest stimulus leads to fastest learning with easy discrimination.
findings.quote: the strongest stimulus (420 units), the most rapid.

findings.mechanism: When discrimination is extremely difficult, learning rapidity increases with stimulus strength from threshold, but then decreases beyond an optimal point (195 units).
findings.quote: both the weak and the strong stimuli were less favorable to the acquirement of the habit than the intermediate stimulus of 195 units.

findings.consequent: Optimal electric stimulus strength for habit-formation
findings.mechanism: As the task becomes more difficult, the optimal level of arousal (stimulus strength) for performance shifts towards lower intensities, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: As the difficultness of discrimination is increased the strength of that stimulus which is most favorable to habit-formation approaches the threshold.

findings.mechanism: More difficult discrimination requires more cognitive effort, slowing down learning.
findings.quote: the rapidity of learning increases as the amount of difference in the brightness of the electric boxes between which the mouse is required to discriminate is increased.

findings.consequent: Errors made from the start of training
findings.mechanism: Stronger initial stimulus may lead to more immediate avoidance behavior, reducing initial errors.
findings.quote: fewer errors are made from the start under the condition of strong stimulation than under the condition of weak stimulation.

mechanisms: The Yerkes-Dodson Law: The relationship between arousal (stimulus strength) and performance (rapidity of habit-formation) is curvilinear, with optimal performance occurring at an intermediate level of arousal. This optimal level shifts depending on task difficulty.
Motivation: Weak stimuli provide insufficient motivation for learning, while excessively strong stimuli may lead to distress or interfere with learning.
Cognitive load: More difficult discrimination tasks require higher cognitive effort, making the organism more sensitive to arousal levels.
implementation_implications: The study highlights the importance of matching the level of stimulation/arousal to the difficulty of a task for optimal learning or performance. For easy tasks, higher stimulation can be beneficial, but for difficult tasks, moderate or even lower stimulation is more effective.

limitations: The exact values of stimuli for Set I were not accurately determined due to lack of a satisfactory measurement means at the time.
The number of animals used per stimulus strength (four mice) was small, potentially leading to irregularities in curves (e.g., slight rise for 375 units in Set II).
The most favorable strength of stimulation for Set I might not have been precisely discovered as only three strengths were used.
The method of controlling visual conditions using cardboards was relatively complicated and difficult to describe, and superior methods were known but not used for comparability with previous work.
